name: Clean eating

card.summary: A whole-foods eating style (the chicken, rice and broccoli staple) that forums link to clearer skin and leaner looks; research on its health effects is limited and has flagged links to disordered eating.
card.note: Studies have associated strict clean-eating beliefs with disordered-eating symptoms in some people.

quick.overview:
Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets built around whole, minimally processed foods and avoiding refined sugar, additives and convenience products. It began in 1990s bodybuilding, where it meant high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals such as chicken, rice and vegetables, and later spread through wellness books and social media.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a baseline for leanness, skin and hormones. Researchers have described the scientific literature on clean eating as thin, with most studies looking at how people define it and how it relates to body image and eating behaviour.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners favour whole foods, simple ingredient lists and less added sugar, sometimes with extra exclusions such as gluten or dairy. Forum users link this to lower insulin spikes, steadier hormones and fewer acne flares; these mechanisms are discussed in the community and have not been tested as a package.
quick.risks: Surveys and qualitative studies have linked rigid clean-eating beliefs with restrained eating and with orthorexia nervosa, a proposed (not formally recognised) eating disorder. Versions that cut out whole food groups have been criticised by commentators for possible nutrient gaps. Analyses of clean-eating blog recipes found nutrient profiles broadly similar to other recipes.

lead: Clean eating is an umbrella term for diets built on whole, minimally processed foods, with fewer convenience products, refined sugars and additives. It has no single agreed definition: in its simplest form it means more vegetables, fruit, lean protein and whole grains, and in stricter forms it also drops gluten, dairy, grains or all processed ingredients [2][1][4].

For appearance, the idea is that a lean physique and clear skin start in the kitchen. In bodybuilding, where the phrase originated in the 1990s, eating clean means lean protein, complex carbohydrates and vegetables (the chicken, rice and broccoli staple) with the aim of getting leaner without losing muscle [2][20]. Forum users extend the same logic to acne, skin quality and hormones, arguing that less refined sugar and fewer high-glycaemic foods mean lower insulin and androgen activity [3].

The term moved from gyms into mainstream wellness through Tosca Reno's Eat-Clean Diet books from 2007, food blogs, television and Instagram hashtags such as #eatclean [2][20][21]. Researchers have described the research base on clean eating as limited. Most published studies are surveys, qualitative work and content analyses of how people define the term and how it relates to body image and eating behaviour, while dietitians' organisations broadly endorse the whole-food core and caution against rigid versions [2][4][8].

chain: Whole foods replace refined, high-sugar convenience foods
Calories and glycaemic load are easier to manage
Leaner body composition and, per proponents, fewer breakouts
angle.text: People use clean eating as a nutrition base for getting lean and for improving skin: bodybuilders use it to cut body fat while keeping muscle, and forum users use it in the hope of fewer acne flares through lower insulin and androgen activity. The benefit comes through overall diet quality and calorie control rather than from a specific food.

paras: There is no single agreed definition. Grokipedia describes the core as whole foods in their natural form, with fresh fruit and vegetables, lean proteins, whole grains and healthy fats, and with refined sugars, artificial additives and preservatives avoided or limited [1]. Reading ingredient labels and preferring short ingredient lists are commonly described habits [1]. Wikipedia notes that some versions also exclude gluten, grains or dairy and that some promote raw food, and flags the definition as disputed [2].

A study asking US undergraduates to define clean eating found that people described it in varied ways, and examined how those perceptions related to disordered-eating indicators [4]. A scoping review of "clean" food labels found that consumers read the word as meaning minimally processed, additive-free, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free or simply natural, with no consensus definition [17]. Because definitions differ, researchers treat clean eating as a loose cluster of beliefs rather than one protocol [2][4].

Wikipedia traces the term to the 1990s bodybuilding community, where it described high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating that avoided sugar, fat and junk food to build muscle without gaining fat [2]. Writer Greg Merritt, recalling that era, describes "clean" as bodybuilding slang for eating like a dieting bodybuilder, which outsiders did not understand; its opposite, eating "dirty", meant something like a pizza on a cheat day [20]. Grokipedia gives an earlier 1980s origin; the sources differ on the decade [1].

In that subculture the meaning was stable: lean protein, complex carbohydrates and vegetables, with white flour, sugar and saturated fat avoided, and the goal of reducing body fat [20]. This is the version most often referenced in the bodybuilding-derived parts of looksmaxxing culture.

subs.h: Tosca Reno and the Eat-Clean books
paras: Canadian author Tosca Reno (born 1959) began as a columnist for Oxygen magazine and met publisher Robert Kennedy, founder of Robert Kennedy Publishing and MuscleMag International, in 2000; the two later married [21]. Her Eat-Clean Diet series began with The Eat-Clean Diet Book and Cookbook in 2007, followed by titles including The Eat-Clean Diet Workout (2008), The Eat-Clean Diet for Men (2009), Recharged (2009) and Stripped (2011); the series has sold more than four million copies, according to her Wikipedia biography [21].

Merritt writes that Reno kept the bodybuilding core of lean protein, complex carbohydrates, weight training and supplements, and added an emphasis on whole, organic food and criticism of processed foods and sugar, which moved the term from hardcore fitness toward general wellness [20]. Kennedy's company later also published a Clean Eating magazine [20].

In the 2010s clean eating became a catch-all label for healthy or natural eating, carried by blogs, television segments, magazines, cookbooks, podcasts and YouTube channels, and by the #eatclean hashtag [2][20]. Wikipedia names Ella Mills, Natasha Corrett and the Hemsley sisters among its advocates [2]. Mills started the Deliciously Ella blog in 2012 and published her first book in 2015; Wikipedia reports she once advocated clean eating and later distanced herself after media criticism [22]. Jasmine and Melissa Hemsley began a recipe blog on Vogue's website in 2012 and published The Art of Eating Well in 2014; they say they have never used the term "clean eating" in their books, though critics have placed them in the movement [23].

Analyses of Instagram and TikTok content have examined how clean-eating and "what I eat in a day" posts present food and bodies [9][10], and an Instagram survey study asked how women engaging with "eat clean, train mean, get lean" fitness imagery felt about body image and health behaviours [6].

Practitioners describe a routine of cooking at home, building meals around a protein source, vegetables and a whole-grain or starchy side, reading labels and avoiding foods with long ingredient lists [1][20]. Bodybuilding versions add meal prepping, repeated staple meals and sometimes a planned "cheat" meal [20]. Wellness versions often add plant-based or gluten-free recipes, smoothies and "free-from" baking [2][22][23].

In looksmaxxing communities the practice is usually framed as a foundation rather than a protocol: a baseline of low-sugar, protein-forward meals on which training, skincare and other measures sit [3].
No clinical trials testing a defined clean-eating diet against a comparison diet for skin or appearance outcomes were found. The available research is observational, survey-based or qualitative.

A cross-sectional analysis of Australian women examined dietary intake, restrained eating and opinions about clean eating [8]. A comparison of nutrient composition assessed recipes from popular clean-eating blogs against recipes without clean-eating claims [7]. A survey of Instagram users studied body image and health behaviours among women engaging with fitspiration and clean-eating imagery [6]. A 2024 systematic review of 38 studies on eating-related social media content found positive relationships between exposure to material such as clean-eating content and body-image concerns or disordered eating, while studies focused on general "healthy food" content showed no such link [5].

For the skin question, Wikipedia's acne article reports that several trials found lower-glycaemic-load diets reduced acne, while evidence on dairy is weaker and observational [14]. These trials tested glycaemic load, not clean eating as a package.

Orthorexia nervosa, a proposed eating disorder describing an obsession with healthy or "clean" eating, is not in the DSM-5 or ICD-11; physician Steven Bratman introduced the term in 1997 [11]. Bratman has stressed that following a dietary theory is not orthorexia in itself, and that the term applies only when an eating disorder develops around it [11]. Dunn and Bratman proposed diagnostic criteria in 2016, centred on an obsessive focus on healthy eating with escalating restriction and clinical impairment [11].

A study of undergraduates examining perceptions of #cleaneating reported associations with indicators of disordered eating [4]. Qualitative work with people showing orthorexic tendencies and an analysis of blogs by women who identified as having orthorexia described rigid rules and distress, and an orthorexia measurement tool, the ONI, was developed using an online sample that included people searching for clean-eating terms [3][12][13]. An observational study in Croatian gym attendees used the ORTHO-15 questionnaire to examine orthorexia symptoms in fitness participants [18]. These studies describe associations and experiences and do not establish that clean eating causes eating disorders. Wikipedia also notes critics' concerns that the main screening tool, ORTO-15, may overstate prevalence [11].

Commentators generally regard the basic idea of eating more whole foods and vegetables and fewer sugary processed foods as sensible, while criticising extreme versions that remove whole food groups for lacking scientific support; one raised concern is lower calcium intake if dairy is avoided [2]. A British Heart Foundation dietitian said whole foods and less processed food are positive for most people, called the term vague, and noted that honey, maple syrup and juices still contribute free sugars; she described the "clean" versus "dirty" framing as presenting an unrealistic image of perfection and advised flexibility [24].

Critiques by Guardian writers Ruby Tandoh and Bee Wilson are cited in Wikipedia's account of the backlash; Merritt's retrospective also lists critics who called the term elitist for favouring expensive organic food, and Wilson linked it to orthorexia [2][20]. Grokipedia notes that marketing labels claiming products are "clean" can mislead and that restrictive versions may bring nutrient deficiencies [1].

Researchers writing in the International Journal of Eating Disorders in 2022 reviewed the public-health side of "clean" food labels, reporting that the US FDA had taken little action on them and that Food Standards Australia New Zealand's position appeared similar; one commentary expected consumer education to be the most efficient response [16][17]. A 2018 Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology piece was titled "When clean eating goes dirty" [19]. A study of blog recipes found nutrient profiles broadly similar between recipes with and without clean-eating claims [7].

The chicken, rice and broccoli staple is a recurring reference point in bodybuilding-derived parts of looksmaxxing culture, where leanness and facial leanness (lower body fat showing more bone structure) are common goals. In one looksmax.org thread, a user asked whether a long-term "clean" diet could change acne through insulin, SHBG and testosterone pathways, and another user in the thread argued that very clean eating might make the body more sensitive to insulin and androgen surges; the thread's author conceded that many other variables, such as sebum composition and the gut microbiome, were involved [3].

timeline.event: Robert Kennedy founds Robert Kennedy Publishing with MuscleMag International, later a publisher of Oxygen and Clean Eating magazines [21][20].
"Eating clean" circulates as bodybuilding slang for lean, high-protein, low-carbohydrate eating [2][20].
Steven Bratman coins the term orthorexia in an article in Yoga Journal [11].
Tosca Reno publishes The Eat-Clean Diet Book and Cookbook, the start of a series that moves the term toward mainstream wellness [21][20].
Deliciously Ella and the Hemsley sisters' recipe blog launch, part of the wellness-blog wave associated with clean eating [22][23].
Ella Mills publishes her first cookbook, Deliciously Ella [22].
Dunn and Bratman propose diagnostic criteria for orthorexia nervosa [11].
Ella Mills' London cafe and deli close with reported debts of 720,000 pounds, around the time of media criticism of clean eating [22].
A study of US undergraduates examines perceptions of #cleaneating and links to disordered eating [4].
International Journal of Eating Disorders publishes a scoping review of "clean" food labels and commentaries from Australia and Europe [17][16][15].
A systematic review of 38 studies links some eating-related social media content, including clean eating, to body-image concerns [5].

lore.intro: Clean eating is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces as a foundation habit for leanness and skin, often alongside bodybuilding-style meal prep [3][20].

claims.claim: Eating clean improves skin and acne
claims.believers: Forum users say cutting refined sugar, high-glycaemic carbs and seed oils lowers insulin and androgen activity and so reduces breakouts [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's acne article reports that several trials found lower-glycaemic-load diets reduced acne, while evidence on dairy is weaker and observational [14]. No trial has tested a defined clean-eating pattern for skin.

claims.claim: A very clean diet makes the body more sensitive to insulin and androgen spikes
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster proposed that a healthier diet increases sensitivity so that occasional junk food triggers larger hormone swings, while admitting the idea was speculative [3].
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing this hypothesis in relation to acne.

claims.claim: Clean eating is the way bodybuilders get lean
claims.believers: Bodybuilders describe eating lean protein, complex carbohydrates and vegetables while avoiding sugar and white flour as the standard way to drop body fat while keeping muscle [20].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's account of the term's origin describes this bodybuilding meaning [2]. Dietitians cited by the BHF say the whole-food core is positive for most people but that the label itself is vague [24].

claims.claim: Clean-eating food is more nutritious than other food
claims.believers: Advocates promote recipes free of refined ingredients as healthier choices [1].
claims.experts: A comparison of nutrient composition between blog recipes with and without clean-eating claims examined this question directly [7]; a cross-sectional study of women also examined dietary intake alongside restrained eating and opinions about clean eating [8].

claims.claim: Clean eating is a safe, flexible lifestyle rather than a diet
claims.believers: Grokipedia and wellness writers describe it as flexible and sustainable rather than restrictive [1].
claims.experts: Research on undergraduates and on people with orthorexic tendencies has found associations between clean-eating beliefs and disordered-eating symptoms in some groups [4][12].

claims.claim: Cutting out gluten and dairy is part of eating clean
claims.believers: Some wellness versions exclude gluten, grains or dairy and treat this as central [2][23].
claims.experts: A BHF dietitian notes that dropping dairy and wheat is often recommended without a diagnosed intolerance, and Wikipedia reports concern about calcium intake if dairy is removed [24][2].

claims.claim: Calling foods clean or dirty is harmless shorthand
claims.believers: Bodybuilders use the pair as plain slang for lean versus indulgent meals [20].
claims.experts: A BHF dietitian says the framing sets up an unrealistic image of perfection [24]; a scoping review found "clean" labels carry no agreed meaning and are unregulated in the US [17][16].
